Q: Is using Entity Framework code first purely for database migrations ok? A:

Yes, you can use Entity Framework only for migrations and continue using Dapper for data access. There is nothing technically wrong with that approach.

The trade-off is that EF migrations still require you to maintain EF-specific infrastructure, including a DbContext, entity mappings, migration classes, and model snapshots. If the project already uses Entity Framework, that may be perfectly reasonable. However, if you chose Dapper specifically because you do not want an EF dependency, maintaining a separate EF model only for migrations may feel unnecessary.

Dapper itself does not provide schema migration support. It focuses on executing queries and mapping results, so schema changes need to be managed by another tool or by versioned SQL scripts.

Another option is to use a standalone schema and migration tool. I maintain an open-source project called ModelSync.

Disclosure: I am the author of ModelSync.

ModelSync is intended for applications that use Dapper, ADO.NET, or hand-written SQL but still need a structured way to manage database schema changes.

It can generate provider-specific table and index SQL from attributed C# models, compare those models with an existing database, run ordered SQL migration scripts, and keep a history of applied migrations.

It also includes a CLI, which can be used locally or from a CI/CD pipeline to validate migration files, preview changes with a dry run, apply migrations explicitly, and generate Markdown or JSON reports.

The stable providers are SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, and SQLite. Oracle support is also available as a preview, but it currently has a smaller feature set. Table and index generation are supported, along with part of the safe model-comparison workflow, while features such as the migration runner, stored procedure synchronization, database reset, and native migration locking are not yet at the same level as the stable providers.

ModelSync is not an ORM and is not intended to replace Dapper. It does not provide LINQ queries, change tracking, repositories, or runtime entity management. Dapper or ADO.NET remains responsible for application data access.

It is also not an exact replacement for EF migrations. Complex data transformations and database-specific changes may still be better handled through manually written, versioned SQL scripts.

So the choice depends on the project:

  • If you already maintain an EF model, using EF only for migrations can be a reasonable solution.

  • If the application is intentionally built around Dapper or ADO.NET and you do not want to maintain EF infrastructure, a standalone schema and migration tool may be a cleaner option.

Q: Relation between starvation freedom and bounded waiting A:

  1. Does starvation-freedom imply deadlock-freedom?
    Yes. Starvation-freedom means every process gets its turn eventually. Deadlock-freedom is a weaker condition, it means some process eventually enters the critical section.

  2. Does starvation-freedom imply bounded-waiting?
    No, because bounded waiting is a stronger condition than starvation-freedom, the later ensures every process enters the critical section eventually, but the former ensures every process enters the cs within a finite bound of turns after it requested entry to the critical section.
    For eg. Two processes: P0, P1
    - On request 1: P1 enters 5 times before P0 gets its turn,
    - On request 2: P1 enters 20 times before P0 gets its turn,
    - On request 2: P1 enters 100 times before P0 gets its turn,
    - On request 2: P1 enters 1000 times before P0 gets its turn,
    Even though P0 is not starved, the number of times P1 enters before P0 can grow without bound (5 → 20 → 100 → 1000...)

  3. Does bounded-waiting imply starvation-freedom?
    No, this one is subtle. Bounded-waiting is usually enough to imply starvation-freedom, because bounded-waiting is a stronger condition than starvation-freedom but it assumes the system as a whole keeps moving, ie. progress is satisfied. Without progress, bounded-waiting is meaning less. For eg. if all the processes get stuck in the entry section then it doesn't matter if bounded-waiting promised entry to every process. Therefore, Progress + Bounded-waiting => Starvation-freedom.

  4. Does bounded-waiting AND deadlock-freedom imply starvation-freedom?
    Yes, bounded-waiting guarantees each progress gets its turn eventually, and deadlock-freedom guarantees that the system as a whole doesn't get stuck and keeps progressing. So, it implies starvation-freedom.

Q: Prisma migration needs default value? A:

Can you see this example from prisma Docs?

model User {
  id          Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  name        String?
  followedBy  User[]   @relation("UserFollows", references: [id])
  following   User[]   @relation("UserFollows", references: [id])
}

Q: How to add a test run to ALM using REST API A:

The way to create a new test execution in the test lab for a given test, is not easy and has to go through 2 API calls in sequence to succeed, and with precise constraints that I will sum up below.

  1. the first API call is a httpPost that will create a test run. But it will not be visible in the test lab ! -don't ask me why. It will be visible in the test execution history of the test only. Furthermore, the api call has, beyond the minimal mandatory fields (test id, cycle id , test set id and a few others...) A SPECIFIC TEMPORARY STATUS that needs to be put : "Not Completed".

  2. the second API call is a httpPut. the real test's status can be put here. This one will make the test result appear in the test lab (and update the test history execution detail).

This solution has been kindly described by mr lobster here : https://lobsterautomation.wordpress.com/2017/01/18/hp-alm-rest-api/ and it has all the details to run successfully. Please praise him for his help !
